C.W. was flat convinced Luther was cheating, but he couldn't prove a lick of it.

Well, that July, Luther got desperate. He drove all the way down to South Carolina, bought a fifty-pound Charleston Gray out of the back of a rusted pickup truck, and hauled it back home under a tarp like it was stolen gold. He buried it out in the middle of his patch, waiting for fair day.

C.W. happened to be up in his barn loft with the binoculars and saw the whole thing plain as day. Now, C.W. didn't run to the sheriff and he didn't start a fistfight. He waited till midnight, crept out there with a pocketknife and a needle and fishing line, and carefully cut the bottom rind off that South Carolina melon.

He scooped out every last seed and red bit of meat, filled the empty green shell to the brim with sixty pounds of slick red river mud and a very ornery, half-grown opossum he’d caught in a trash can, and stitched that rind back on tighter than a drum.

Come fair morning, Luther hoisted that melon onto the scales with a crowd watching. The judge dropped the blade to cut the first slice, and that possum came through the rind screaming bloody murder, covered in red mud, and bit the judge right on the thumb. Luther didn't win the blue ribbon that year, but he did win a fast trip to the county clinic, and C.W. bought himself a brand-new John Deere with the money he won betting against him.

But right about the time Earl was figuring out how much the taxidermist was going to charge him, a massive wave hit sideways, the line snapped tight with a crack like a dry pine tree, and the entire rear bumper of that Ford came clean off, flying through the air and landing twenty feet out in the breaker zone.

The fish kept right on going, and Earl ended up sitting alone in his lawn chair in two feet of salt water, holding a broken rod and watching his truck’s rear bumper swim away toward the Gulf Stream. To this day, Ray swears it was a five-hundred-pound shark, but Earl just won't talk about it unless you promise not to mention chrome bumpers.

Earl wasn’t a man for half-measures, so he didn’t just bring a standard surf rod; he brought a five-gallon bucket of fresh mullet, a folding recliner he wired to a piece of plywood so it wouldn't sink in the wet sand, and a heavy-duty reel that looked like a winch off a log truck.

Well, about high tide, something hit Earl’s line that didn’t just take bait, it took offense. That fish started pulling south toward Cape Point like it had an appointment in Ocracoke, and Earl dug his heels into the sand. When he realized he was sliding backward out to sea in his lawn chair, he didn't let go of the rod. Instead, he hollered at Ray to run up to the dunes and tie the heavy leader line directly to the trailer hitch of Earl’s old Ford pickup truck.

Ray threw it in four-wheel drive and started crawling up the beach, dragging that fish through the surf. They thought they had him licked. But right about the time Earl was figuring out how much the taxidermist was going to charge him, a massive wave hit sideways, the line snapped tight with a crack like a dry pine tree, and the entire rear bumper of that Ford came clean off, flying through the air and landing twenty feet out in the breaker zone.

The fish kept right on going, and Earl ended up sitting alone in his lawn chair in two feet of salt water, holding a broken rod and watching his truck’s rear bumper swim away toward the Gulf Stream. To this day, Ray swears it was a five-hundred-pound shark, but Earl just won't talk about it unless you promise not to mention chrome bumpers.

Back in nineteen-eighty-four, a fellow named Earl Jenkins bought himself a five-year-old gelding down at the livestock market in Monroe, swearing blind he was getting the best cutting horse in Union County. The seller told Earl the horse had cost a fortune in training and could turn on a dime, which sounded mighty fine until Earl tried to work him on the farm the very next Tuesday.

That horse, whose name was General, didn't care a lick about cattle or fence lines. He stood square in the middle of the red dirt, dropped his head, and refused to budge an inch no matter how much Earl hollered or waved his hat. By sundown, Earl had tried sugar cubes, gentle coaxing, and finally a mighty stern lecture, but General just stood there chewing a mouthful of clover like he owned the county courthouse.

About dusk, the man Earl bought him from rode past on a mule and stopped at the fence line. Earl was red-faced and soaked through with sweat, leaning on a shovel. The fellow looked at General, shook his head, and said he forgot to mention one small detail. General wasn't broken for working land; he was raised as a parade horse for the Shriners, and he wouldn't take a single step forward unless a brass band was playing loud enough to rattle the teeth in his head.

Earl didn't say a word. He walked into the shed, came back out with his old transistor radio tuned straight to the Saturday polka hour at full blast, and tied it securely to the saddle horn. General pranced all the way back to the barn at a high-stepping trot, and Earl hasn't missed a small-town parade in Marshville since.

Back in nineteen seventy-two, old man Clyde Abernathy got it into his head that Miss Lurlene’s towering papershell pecan tree was dropping its bounty across the property line, and by God, a stray pecan falling on Clyde's soil belonged to Clyde. Lurlene, who could skin a catfish faster than you can blink and didn’t take sass from nobody in Harnett County, told him if a squirrel carried a pecan over there, he was welcome to go negotiate with the squirrel.

Clyde didn't want to deal with squirrels. Instead, he spent three sweltering days hauling corrugated sheet metal and cedar posts out to the fence line, building a ten-foot wall to intercept Lurlene’s tree. He stood back on the fourth afternoon, wiping sweat with a red bandanna, purely tickled with himself. He figured he’d have enough pecans by Friday to bake three pies and still have leftovers to trade for a gallon of cider.

That night, a sudden squall blew in off the river, howling fierce enough to wake the dead. That sheet metal wall Clyde built didn’t have a lick of bracing, and it acted just like a brand-new sail on a square-rigger.

About midnight, there was a terrible screech of rusted nails pulling free, followed by a heavy thud that rattled the jam jars on Clyde's back porch. When the sun came up, that ten-foot wall hadn’t just fallen over. It had sheared clean through Clyde's prized greenhouse, flattened forty hills of his best Beefmaster tomatoes, and landed square in the middle of Lurlene’s yard, completely missing the pecan tree. Lurlene walked out in her house slippers, picked up a single unbroken tomato off the heap, took a bite, and hollered across the wreck that the soil over on Clyde's side was finally good for something.

Luther and his brother-in-law J.D. got into it down at the Red Oak crossroads over a homing pigeon J.D. claimed he bought off a fella up in Emporia. J.D. swore that bird, which he called General Beauregard, had a compass built right into its beak and could find its way home from the moon if you gave it half a chance. Luther didn't believe a word of it, seeing as how J.D. couldn't find his own truck in a grocery store parking lot without a flare gun. They put ten silver dollars on the tailgate of a Ford pickup to settle the hash.

Next morning, J.D. loaded the General into a ventilated shoebox, drove forty miles down past Tarboro, and turned him loose right by the river bridge. He drove back home feeling mighty proud of himself, waiting for that feathered Einstein to show up on the back porch. Two days went by, and nary a feather was to be seen. Luther started dropping by just to ask if the General had sent a postcard yet, and J.D. was running out of excuses to give his wife.

On the fourth morning, Luther walked out on his back porch to fetch the paper, and there sat General Beauregard on the railing, looking like he had flown through a hailstorm and lost a personal argument with a combine. Tied right around his skinny left leg with a piece of binder twine was a little blue slip of paper. Luther picked it up and squinted at it. It was a receipt for a whole fried chicken and a cherry soda from the lunch counter down in Rocky Mount, time-stamped just three hours earlier.

Well, I'd love to tell you a story. 

Back in the winter of nineteen and fifty-eight, out near a little crossroads called Micro, my granddaddy had a hound dog named Blue. Blue wasn't much to look at—mostly hound with a crooked tail and ears that dragged in the briars—but that dog thought he owned the county. 

One freezing Friday night, Granddaddy woke up to a terrible racket out by the smokehouse. He figured a stray fox or a possum had gotten into the feed bags, so he pulled on his heavy wool coat over his flannel shirt, grabbed his old flashlight—the big heavy metal kind that took those three-cell batteries and weighed about five pounds—and stepped out onto the porch. The ground was just crunchy with a hard white frost, and your breath hung in the air like steam off a kettle.

He walked out past the well house, shining that beam along the edge of the woods, and called out, "Blue? You old fool, what are you getting into now?" 

Well, the light caught a pair of green eyes shining back from the lower branch of an old water oak. But it wasn't a possum, and it wasn't a coon. It was a bobcat, big as a butter tub, just sitting up there looking down at Blue, who was treeing at the trunk and carrying on like he was auditioning for the church choir. 

Granddaddy stood there in the dark, trying to figure out how to get a stubborn hound and a very annoyed bobcat untangled without getting himself clawed, when suddenly the back door flew open. Out came my grandmother in her house slippers and a heavy quilt wrapped around her shoulders, holding a cast-iron skillet like she was fixing to fry up a mess of catfish. 

She took one look at the cat, looked at Granddaddy, and didn't say a word. She just walked right past him, banged that iron skillet against the oak tree trunk with a *clang* that you could've probably heard clean over in Johnston County, and hollered, "You get on back to the swamp where you belong, before I make a rug out of you!" 

That bobcat looked at Granddaddy, looked at Grandma with that skillet, and decided discretion was the better part of valor. It turned tail and scrambled up higher into the dark woods faster than greased lightning. Blue gave two more half-hearted yips, and Grandma turned around, looked at my granddaddy shivering in his boots, and said, "Well, are you fixing to stand out here all night freezing your ears off, or are you coming in for some hot coffee?" 

And Granddaddy, he just laughed, picked up the hound by his collar, and told her yes ma'am, he was right behind her.
